* * * [T]he court agrees that Rule 412 governs the admissibility of evidence at trial, and that relevance is not equivalent to admissibility. In
fact, the Advisory Committee Notes to the 1994 amendments to Rule 412 are quite explicit in this respect. * * * [T]he proper inquiry at this
juncture is whether the information sought from [the student] is discoverable, keeping in mind relevance, proportionality, and [the student’s]
interests in assuring confidentiality and preventing unwarranted inquiries into her sexual conduct.
2.Prior to 2015, Rule 26(b)(1) set forth a two-tier approach to the discoverability of relevant information. The first tier defined relevance with
respect to any claim or defense of a party, and information was discoverable without a court order. The second tier defined relevance with respect to the
subject matter of the dispute, and disclosure required a court order upon a showing of good cause. The two-tier approach, adopted in 2000, replaced
earlier language that had allowed discovery, without a court order, of information relevant to the subject matter of the dispute. The 2015 amendment
eliminated any reference to subject-matter discovery and the court no longer has discretion to order disclosure of such information. However, the
Advisory Committee Note to the 2015 amendment states that the rule change does not foreclose discovery of information “not directly pertinent to the
incident” as the Advisory Committee had explained when it adopted the two-tier approach in 2000.
Thus, for example, O’GARA v. EQUIFAX INFORMATION SERVICES, LLC, 2018 WL 51335, *9 (S.D.IND. 2018), INVOLVED CLAIMS
UNDER THE FAIR CREDIT REPORTING ACT. PLAINTIFF ALLEGED THAT DEFENDANT USED A MATCHING SYSTEM THAT
WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED HIS FATHER’S TAX ARREARS TO HIM, AND THAT AS A RESULT HE WAS DENIED CREDIT. BY
INTERROGATORY, PLAINTIFF SOUGHT INFORMATION ABOUT THE NUMBER OF CREDIT DISPUTES DEFENDANT HAD
INVESTIGATED AS A RESULT OF “MIXED” FILES. THE DISTRICT COURT REJECTED DEFENDANT’S OBJECTION THAT THE
INFORMATION WAS NOT RELEVANT TO THE CLAIMS AND DEFENSES; TO THE CONTRARY, RELEVANCE WAS ESTABLISHED
BECAUSE THE INFORMATION SOUGHT WAS ABOUT “INCIDENTS OF THE SAME TYPE.” DID THE DISTRICT COURT IN FASSETT, P.
905, SUPRA, ADOPT A SIMILAR APPROACH?
3.Some district courts have held that under the 2015 version of Rule 26(b)(1), “[r]elevance is still to be ‘construed broadly to encompass any
matter that bears on, or that reasonably could lead to other matter that could bear on’ any party’s claim or defense.” State Farm Mutual Auto. Ins. Co.
v. Fayda, 2015 WL 871037, *2 (S.D.N.Y. 2015), quoting Oppenheimer Fund, Inc. v. Sanders, 437 U.S. 340, 351, 98 S.Ct. 2380, 2389, 57 L.Ed.2d 253,
265 (1978). Other district courts have rejected this reading, arguing that it mistakenly equates relevance with subject-matter discovery. See Cole’s
